prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and practically motivated problem: extracting product attributes in an open-world setting with only light supervision. The authors argue, convincingly, that existing formulations are either closed-world, require explicit specification of unseen attribute types at inference time, or depend on noisier distant supervision. In contrast, the proposed setting asks the model to both expand known seed attribute vocabularies and discover entirely new attribute types automatically. This is a meaningful step toward realistic e-commerce information extraction, and the paper’s emphasis on reducing annotation burden is well aligned with industrial needs.

The paper’s main strengths are the task formulation, the dataset construction effort, and the overall system design that combines explicit seed supervision with implicit contextual regularization. The proposed pipeline is intuitive and reasonably well motivated: syntax-based candidate span generation, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed values, adaptive expansion for known attributes, and clustering for residual candidates. The additional use of self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence and latent-attribute regularization is the most novel modeling component, and the empirical results suggest that these signals help especially on unseen attribute types. The reported gains over OA-Mine and other baselines are substantial on the proposed benchmark, and the decomposition by seed/new types and title/bullet-point subsets is useful.

That said, I have several concerns about the formulation, evaluation, and empirical validation that limit my confidence in the strength of the conclusions.

First, the paper introduces a new task and a new dataset simultaneously, which makes it difficult to disentangle whether the gains reflect genuine progress on open-world attribute mining or optimization toward a benchmark whose assumptions favor the proposed pipeline. The dataset appears thoughtfully constructed, but many design choices embed strong inductive biases that align closely with the method. In particular, the seed set is derived from Amazon product profiles and then matched back into the corpus by string matching; candidate span generation also derives valid POS patterns from product-profile attribute values. This means both supervision and candidate extraction are partially bootstrapped from the same source distribution. While this is practical, it raises the possibility that the benchmark rewards methods that exploit profile-like phrase regularities rather than truly open-world semantic discovery. The paper would be stronger with a clearer discussion of this coupling and with experiments showing robustness when seed construction and candidate-pattern induction are perturbed or sourced differently.

Second, the candidate generation stage is both crucial and somewhat under-evaluated. The paper argues that syntax-oriented POS patterns outperform segmentation and are more suitable for bullet points, which is plausible. However, because the entire downstream pipeline depends on candidate quality, the method’s success may be driven substantially by this handcrafted/bootstrapped filtering stage rather than by the representation learning innovations. Table 5 indeed shows that span extraction quality remains quite low in absolute terms, especially exact-match precision. This suggests that the candidate stage is still noisy and perhaps the dominant bottleneck. I would have liked a much more thorough intrinsic evaluation of candidate generation: candidate recall against gold spans, precision/recall by category, effect of the number of POS patterns, sensitivity to POS tagging errors, and comparison to simpler noun-phrase chunking or constituency-based extraction baselines. As written, the paper claims the syntax stage is “basic yet effective,” but the evidence is mostly indirect.

Third, the evaluation protocol is somewhat problematic. The paper uses clustering metrics such as Jaccard, ARI, and NMI on gold spans, plus recall, and then defines a “pseudo-F1” by averaging Jaccard/ARI/NMI as pseudo-precision and combining with recall. This aggregate metric is not standard and lacks a clear theoretical interpretation. Since these clustering metrics capture different properties and are not calibrated as precision surrogates, averaging them and then computing an F1-like score may distort comparisons. The paper does report the underlying metrics, which is good, but the headline claims rely heavily on this pseudo-F1. I would strongly encourage the authors to justify this metric more carefully, or better, to report a more standard evaluation decomposition: span detection precision/recall/F1, cluster purity/completeness, B-cubed or CEAF-style clustering metrics, and separate evaluation for known-type expansion versus novel-type discovery. The current metric makes it hard to assess what exactly improves: extraction, clustering purity, cluster coverage, or some mixture.

Relatedly, the partial-match criterion is sensible for open-world extraction, but the exact definition (“more than half of the span falls into a gold value”) seems asymmetric and potentially permissive. It would help to clarify whether overlap is measured token-wise, whether matching is one-to-one, and how duplicate predictions are handled. Since many gains appear larger under partial match, these details matter.

Fourth, the novelty of the modeling contribution is moderate rather than high. The system is a sensible composition of known ingredients: BERT span embeddings, supervised contrastive learning, adaptive thresholding against seed sets, DBSCAN, a skip-gram-like co-occurrence regularizer, and neural topic-model-inspired latent variables. The latent attribute component is the most distinctive piece, but even there the formulation is fairly close to embedded topic models adapted from prior work. The contribution is therefore more in task adaptation and system integration than in fundamentally new methodology. That is acceptable for an applied or resource-oriented paper, but the paper occasionally overstates novelty, especially around “novel formulation” claims. A more measured positioning would improve credibility.

Fifth, some methodological details are underspecified or potentially questionable. For example, in the supervised contrastive loss, the denominator appears to sum only over negatives rather than over all non-anchor examples including positives, which differs from the standard supervised contrastive formulation. If intentional, this should be justified; if not, the equation may be incorrect. Similarly, the adaptive expansion threshold is based on average pairwise cosine distance within the support set, scaled by delta. Intuitively this makes sense, but there is little analysis of why this thresholding is stable across attributes with very different intra-class variance or seed-set sizes. Since the seed sets average only 22 values per type and are frequency-truncated, some attributes may be much more heterogeneous than others. A calibration analysis would be useful.

Sixth, the empirical scope is somewhat narrow. The dataset covers only four categories, all from Amazon, all in English, and all with full descriptions available. This is a reasonable starting point, but it limits claims about general open-world product attribute mining. The paper mentions degradation on user-generated content datasets, but this is only briefly referenced and not fully integrated into the main evaluation. Given the practical motivation, cross-domain robustness is critical. I would have liked to see stronger transfer experiments: train on one subset of categories and test on another, evaluate on noisier marketplaces or reviews, or at least compare title-only versus bullet-only training more systematically. Without such evidence, it is hard to know whether the method generalizes beyond relatively clean retailer-authored descriptions.

Seventh, the annotation protocol for new attribute types deserves more scrutiny. Annotators are asked to label spans that are “reasonable attribute values” of either existing or brand-new types that “fit the context.” This leaves substantial room for subjectivity, especially in deciding what counts as an attribute versus a general descriptive phrase, and in defining the granularity of new types. The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, adjudication procedures, or examples of ambiguous cases beyond a few qualitative illustrations. Since the task’s open-world nature makes ontology boundaries fuzzy, annotation consistency is central. The absence of agreement statistics is a significant weakness for a dataset paper.

Eighth, the comparison to baselines is useful but not entirely comprehensive or fully fair. The strongest baseline, OA-Mine, is adapted in multiple ways, which is appreciated. However, there are several missing comparisons that would help isolate contributions: a noun-phrase extraction plus SBERT clustering baseline; a prompt-based or embedding-based zero-shot baseline using attribute names where available; a simpler pseudo-labeling/self-training baseline from seed matches; and ablations replacing the latent attribute model with generic unsupervised contrastive objectives over product context. Since the proposed method is a pipeline, stronger modular baselines are important. Also, the closed-world tagging baselines are expected to underperform on new-type discovery by construction, so their inclusion is less informative than stronger open extraction baselines.

Ninth, the paper’s own qualitative analysis reveals a central limitation: many new-type values are extracted but then absorbed into existing seed clusters rather than forming coherent new clusters. This is arguably the hardest part of the task, and the current method only partially solves it. Discovering values from 39% of unseen attribute types is promising, but it also means most unseen types remain undiscovered. The paper would benefit from a more explicit error taxonomy: failures due to missing candidates, boundary errors, semantic confusion with existing types, cluster fragmentation, and topic collapse in latent attributes. Such analysis would help readers understand where future progress is needed.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has real merit. The problem is important, the dataset appears valuable, and the method is practical. The strongest empirical takeaway is not necessarily that the latent-attribute regularizer is a breakthrough, but that combining modest seed supervision with syntax-aware candidate generation and contextual regularization can materially improve open-world attribute mining under realistic constraints. That is a useful contribution.

For improvement, I would recommend the following. First, strengthen the dataset section with inter-annotator agreement, clearer annotation guidelines for new types, and examples of borderline cases. Second, provide intrinsic evaluation of candidate generation and sensitivity analyses for POS patterns and tagging noise. Third, reconsider the main metric or at least supplement it with more standard clustering and extraction metrics. Fourth, add stronger ablations and simpler baselines to isolate the gains from each component, especially the latent attribute module. Fifth, discuss more explicitly the dependence on Amazon profiles and whether this introduces benchmark-specific bias. Sixth, if possible, include cross-domain or cross-category transfer results to support broader claims of practicality.

In summary, this is a solid and practically motivated paper with a valuable new task setting and promising empirical results, but the methodological novelty is moderate and several aspects of evaluation and dataset validation need to be strengthened. My overall assessment is cautiously positive if the venue values practical open-world IE and dataset contributions, but I would want the authors to address the concerns above before fully endorsing the stronger claims.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting, where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover values for previously unseen attribute types without explicitly naming them. To support this setting, the authors construct the WoaM dataset over four Amazon product categories with seed attributes, raw corpus, and human-annotated test data. They propose Amacer, a pipeline consisting of syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for assigning candidates to seed types, DBSCAN for discovering additional clusters, and two auxiliary regularizers for unseen attributes: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive loss and a neural latent-attribute topic-model-like objective. Experiments show improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines on their dataset, especially in partial-match F1 and new-attribute discovery.
strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting: open-world attribute mining with limited supervision and without requiring explicit descriptions of unseen target attributes.

The dataset contribution appears meaningful: WoaM includes titles and bullet points, multiple categories, and a substantial proportion of unseen attribute types and values, making the benchmark more realistic than title-only settings.
The overall system design is intuitive and modular, combining candidate generation, representation learning, and clustering in a way that matches the task structure.
The syntax-based candidate generation is simple, scalable, and empirically stronger than segmentation-based alternatives in the reported experiments.

The use of additional implicit supervision for unseen attributes is a sensible idea; the latent-attribute regularization is a potentially interesting adaptation of neural topic modeling to span-level attribute discovery.
The empirical study includes multiple baselines, ablations, exact/partial span matching, and decomposed analyses for seed vs. new attributes and title vs. bullet-point text.
Qualitative examples and error analysis are helpful and show both the promise and limitations of the approach.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate: several components are adaptations of existing ideas (supervised contrastive learning, DBSCAN, topic-model-like latent variables, heuristic co-occurrence regularization), and the main contribution is more in task formulation and system integration than in fundamentally new methodology.

The evaluation protocol is somewhat ad hoc. The main metric is a pseudo-F1 built from averaging Jaccard/ARI/NMI as a proxy for precision and combining it with recall, which lacks a clear theoretical justification and may be hard to interpret.

The paper relies heavily on candidate span generation quality, yet the candidate extraction stage still has low precision/recall and may dominate downstream performance; this weakens claims about true open-world attribute understanding.
The dataset scope is limited to four product categories from Amazon and English text only, so generalization to broader domains or languages is unclear.

Comparison to prior work is not entirely clean because some baselines are adapted to a different candidate generation regime, and some gains may come from stronger candidate extraction rather than better clustering or representation learning.
The paper acknowledges performance decline on user-generated content datasets, suggesting limited robustness outside the curated product-description domain.
The discovered new attributes are often confused with existing seed attributes, indicating that the method may still be better at broad semantic grouping than true novel attribute induction.
methodological_flaws: The supervised contrastive loss formulation appears incorrect or at least nonstandard. In Eq. for L^su, the denominator sums only over N^s(i)=I^s\P^s(i), which seems to include the anchor itself and excludes positives from the normalization. Standard supervised contrastive loss typically normalizes over all other examples except the anchor. As written, this could distort optimization and makes the mathematical description questionable.

The same issue appears in the self-supervised contrastive loss L^ss: the denominator uses only negatives from different bullet points, excluding positives and potentially including the anchor depending on indexing. This is again inconsistent with standard InfoNCE-style formulations and weakens confidence in the stated objective.

The latent-variable formulation is mathematically under-specified. Eq. (3) writes mean/variance as a linear projection but does not ensure positivity of variance; in practice one would predict log-variance or apply a softplus. As written, sampling from N(mu, sigma) with unconstrained sigma is invalid.

The KL term in Eq. (8) is not rigorously specified. The notation KL(\tilde{\alpha}^p || \hat{\alpha}) mixes a sampled Gaussian latent variable / logistic-normal parameterization with a standard Gaussian prior, but \tilde{\alpha}^p is later transformed by softmax into simplex probabilities. It is unclear whether the KL is computed in Gaussian pre-softmax space or probability simplex space; the notation suggests a mismatch.

The reconstruction objective for latent attributes uses only positive observed spans in V(p) without discussing normalization for repeated spans, absent spans, or document length effects. This may bias learning toward frequent spans and products with more candidates.

The adaptive expansion threshold uses average pairwise cosine distance within the seed support set. If cosine denotes distance, larger values mean less similarity; then accepting candidates with D(c_i,S_j) < t_j depends on seed-set dispersion in a way that is not well justified. If cosine actually means cosine similarity, the inequality direction is wrong. The notation conflates cosine distance and cosine similarity in multiple places.

The main evaluation metric ('pseudo-F1') is not a standard scientifically validated measure. Averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as pseudo precision and combining with recall may produce misleading rankings, especially since these clustering metrics have different scales and semantics.

Statistical significance claims are weakly supported. The paper mentions a t-test with >95% confidence, but it is unclear what the independent samples are (categories? runs?), and with only four categories the assumptions behind a t-test are dubious.

Because the seed set, POS patterns, and development data are all derived from related product-profile resources, there is a risk of dataset construction bias and leakage of annotation conventions into both candidate generation and tuning. The paper does not fully quantify how much performance depends on this shared source.

Empirical validity for open-world discovery is only partial: the paper reports discovering values from 39% of new types, but many new-type values are either missed or absorbed into existing clusters. This suggests the method may not yet substantiate strong claims of automatic new attribute type discovery.
